subtopic_detail: Abrupt pallor and lethargy after a facial rash illness in a child with a known red cell disorder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7 year old girl with hereditary spherocytosis brought in by her father because she has gone very pale and will not get off the couch. She had a bright red rash on both cheeks and a lacy rash on her arms about a week ago, which her father assumed was heat rash.

Her baseline haemoglobin at clinic three months ago was 108 g/L with a reticulocyte count of 210 x10^9/L. Her father says her eyes look less yellow than usual rather than more. She has had no dark urine, no abdominal pain and no fever today, and her spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, unchanged from her clinic record. Two other children at her school have had a similar facial rash this month.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked pallor of conjunctivae and palms, soft flow murmur, spleen 3 cm below costal margin, no jaundice, no petechiae or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 54 g/L (115-155), reticulocytes 6 x10^9/L (50-100), white cell count 6.1 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-450), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the single most important investigation to confirm the underlying cause?

options.text: Parvovirus B19 serology together with polymerase chain reaction testing on a blood sample
options.rationale: A slapped cheek illness followed by profound anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count in a child with chronic haemolysis is transient aplastic crisis, in which parvovirus B19 arrests erythroid precursors for about a week. Serology plus nucleic acid testing confirms it, and testing matters because it identifies the household infection risk to pregnant contacts and to other children with haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Repeat direct antiglobulin testing with an eluate to identify a warm autoimmune haemolytic process
options.rationale: Autoimmune haemolysis raises the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates and typically gives a positive antiglobulin test with rising bilirubin. Here the reticulocytes are suppressed, bilirubin is low and the antiglobulin test is already negative. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to look for infiltration by a haematological malignancy
options.rationale: Marrow infiltration usually depresses more than one lineage and is accompanied by bruising, bone pain, lymphadenopathy or an abnormal white cell picture. A normal white cell and platelet count with an isolated red cell arrest after a viral exanthem does not warrant an invasive marrow test. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound with splenic measurement to assess for acute sequestration within the spleen
options.rationale: Splenic sequestration causes a rapidly enlarging spleen with a falling haemoglobin and a high reticulocyte count as the marrow responds. This spleen is unchanged from the clinic record and the reticulocyte count has collapsed. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation to assess for coexisting iron deficiency anaemia
options.rationale: Iron deficiency develops over months with microcytosis and does not produce a fall to this level within a week. Chronic haemolysis also tends towards iron loading rather than depletion once transfusions begin. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors and halts red cell production for roughly a week, which is clinically silent in a child with a normal red cell lifespan but catastrophic when the lifespan is already shortened by hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia or sickle cell disease. The signature is severe anaemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, and bilirubin often falls rather than rises because haemolysis is not increased. This inverted pattern is the key discriminator from a haemolytic crisis, splenic sequestration or autoimmune haemolysis, all of which drive reticulocytosis. Treatment is supportive with transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, and marrow recovery follows within one to two weeks. Confirming parvovirus also triggers contact advice, since infection in pregnancy risks foetal hydrops and infection in other children with haemolytic disorders risks the same crisis.
key_points: Anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count after a viral exanthem indicates red cell aplasia
Bilirubin falls in aplastic crisis because haemolysis is not increased
Rising reticulocytes point instead to haemolysis, sequestration or bleeding
Management is supportive with transfusion; the marrow recovers in one to two weeks
Confirmation drives contact tracing for pregnant women and other haemolytic patients
explanation.pearls: The child is most infectious in the week before the facial rash appears and is generally no longer infectious once the rash is visible, so exclusion at rash onset achieves little, while a pregnant household contact who was exposed in the preceding week needs parvovirus serology and foetal surveillance arranged.

subtopic_detail: Worsening bow legs in a heavy toddler beyond the age of expected remodelling
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3 year old boy referred because his legs bow outwards. His mother says other people have started commenting and that it looks worse now than when he began walking at eleven months.

He weighs above the 97th centile for age and his height is on the 50th centile. Standing with the medial malleoli together, the gap between the knees measures 7 cm, and the bowing is more pronounced on the left than the right. As he walks you notice the left knee thrusts outwards during stance. He has no bone pain, no fractures and no dental problems, and he drinks around 600 mL of full cream cow milk daily alongside a varied diet with fish and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Intercondylar distance 7 cm with asymmetry left greater than right, lateral thrust of the left knee during stance phase, no wrist or costochondral widening, no frontal bossing, weight above 97th centile, height 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.55 mmol/L (1.10-1.95), alkaline phosphatase 260 U/L (children 100-400), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe night splints for both legs and arrange physiotherapy to correct the walking pattern
options.rationale: Night splinting has no role in either physiological varus or in a progressive physeal deformity, and the abnormal gait is a consequence of the bony alignment rather than a learned pattern. Bracing that is used for infantile tibia vara is a specific daytime knee ankle foot orthosis prescribed after imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Arrange standing long leg alignment radiographs and refer to paediatric orthopaedics for review
options.rationale: Bowing that is asymmetrical, worsening after the age at which physiological varus should be correcting, and accompanied by a lateral thrust in a heavy child points to a growth disturbance of the proximal tibial physis rather than a normal variant. Standing alignment films quantify the deformity and allow the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle to be measured, and orthopaedic input is needed because bracing or osteotomy may be required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Reassure the family that the alignment corrects spontaneously and arrange review in twelve months
options.rationale: Physiological varus is symmetrical and is correcting by around two years towards neutral and then valgus, so worsening asymmetrical bowing at three years falls outside that pattern. Waiting a further year allows a progressive physeal deformity to become harder to correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Commence high dose oral colecalciferol with elemental calcium supplementation and repeat bloods
options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is excluded by a normal corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level together with the absence of wrist widening or costochondral swelling. Supplementing a replete child treats no deficiency and delays the correct assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Refer for a skeletal survey and genetic assessment to investigate a possible underlying bone dysplasia
options.rationale: A skeletal dysplasia is suggested by short stature with a height well below the expected range for the family and by disproportionate limb segments. This child's height is on the 50th centile, which makes a generalised dysplasia unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable arc, with physiological varus at the start of walking correcting towards neutral by about two years and passing through a valgus phase before settling near adult alignment by about seven years. Departures from that arc are what matter, and the concerning features are asymmetry, progression rather than improvement, an intercondylar distance beyond about 6 cm, short stature, bone pain and a lateral thrust of the knee during stance. Infantile tibia vara affects the medial proximal tibial physis, is strongly associated with high body mass and early walking, and produces exactly this asymmetrical progressive picture. Nutritional rickets is the main metabolic alternative and is screened for with calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D, which are normal here. Standing long leg radiographs with orthopaedic referral is the correct pathway once the presentation leaves the physiological arc.
key_points: Physiological varus corrects by around two years and is symmetrical and painless
Asymmetry, progression and a lateral knee thrust indicate a physeal growth disturbance
High body mass and early walking are the recognised associations of infantile tibia vara
Normal calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D exclude nutritional rickets
Standing long leg alignment films are the imaging of choice, not knee views alone
explanation.pearls: Measure the intercondylar distance with the medial malleoli touching and record it in the notes at each visit, because a gap that is widening across two visits after the second birthday is a more reliable trigger for radiographs than any single measurement, and the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle can then be calculated from a standing film to separate tibia vara from persistent physiological varus.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: Nipple pain and poor weight gain attributed to a restrictive lingual frenulum
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12 day old girl in the breastfeeding support clinic. Her mother has bleeding cracked nipples, describes a shooting pain through the whole feed, and has been told by a family member that the baby needs her tongue tie cut.

Birth weight was 3420 g, weight on day four was 3140 g and today she is 3180 g. She feeds every two hours for around fifty minutes and her mother hears clicking. When you examine the mouth, the frenulum inserts close to the tip of the tongue, the tongue tip notches when she cries, and she cannot lift the tongue above mid mouth or extend it past the lower gum with the mouth wide. A trained lactation consultant has already worked with the pair through two full feeds over two days, correcting positioning and attachment, and the pain and the clicking persist unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum inserting near the tongue tip with notching on crying, tongue elevation restricted to below mid mouth, unable to extend past the lower gum, palate intact, jaw and lip movement normal
data_table.Investigations: Weight 3180 g today, birth weight 3420 g, day four weight 3140 g, six to eight heavy nappies daily, serum bilirubin not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe topical antifungal treatment for mother and infant for suspected candidal nipple infection
options.rationale: Candidal nipple pain classically begins after a period of comfortable feeding and is burning pain persisting between feeds, often with a shiny areola. Pain present from the outset with clicking and poor transfer points to a mechanical problem instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for division of the upper lip frenulum in addition to arranging an oral motor therapy programme
options.rationale: Evidence for division of the upper lip frenulum to improve breastfeeding is weak and the practice is not recommended in Australian paediatric guidance. Adding an unproven procedure and a therapy programme delays the intervention with the best evidence. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Refer for frenotomy with continued lactation support and planned weight review after the procedure
options.rationale: Frenotomy is offered when an anatomically restrictive frenulum is coupled with a demonstrated feeding problem that has not responded to skilled lactation support, which is exactly this pair after two days of hands on work. The procedure is quick and low risk in a young infant, and continued lactation support afterwards is what converts the anatomical change into improved transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Continue lactation support alone for a further two weeks and reassess the feeding at that point
options.rationale: Skilled support is the correct first step and has already been delivered across two days without change, while the infant remains below birth weight at twelve days. Repeating an intervention that has failed risks established low supply and early weaning. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Advise complete transfer to expressed milk by bottle to allow the nipple damage to heal fully
options.rationale: Full transfer to expressed feeding is a reasonable temporary rescue for severe damage but does not address the restriction and commonly ends direct breastfeeding altogether. It also adds a substantial expressing burden without treating the cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia is common and most infants with a visible frenulum feed perfectly well, so the decision to divide rests on function rather than appearance. The threshold combines an anatomically restrictive frenulum, demonstrated by limited tongue elevation and extension with notching of the tip, and a feeding problem such as persistent nipple pain and damage, clicking, prolonged feeds and inadequate weight gain. Crucially, skilled lactation assessment must come first, since positioning and attachment correction resolves the majority of nipple pain without any procedure. Where support has been delivered and the problem persists, frenotomy is a quick low risk office procedure that improves maternal nipple pain most consistently, and lactation follow up afterwards is essential. Division of the upper lip frenulum is not supported and posterior tongue tie remains a contested entity.
key_points: Appearance alone never justifies frenotomy; function plus anatomy does
Skilled lactation support must be delivered and shown to fail first
Restricted elevation and extension with tip notching define an anatomical restriction
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after division
Upper lip frenulum division is not recommended for breastfeeding difficulty
explanation.pearls: Weight against birth weight is the objective anchor in these consultations: an infant who has not regained birth weight by day fourteen has a feeding problem requiring action regardless of the frenulum, while a thriving infant with an obvious tongue tie and comfortable feeding needs no procedure at all.

subtopic_detail: Widespread itchy eruption with palmar involvement in an infant under two months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7 week old boy whose parents report he has been scratching and unsettled for two weeks and that a rash has spread over him. His mother has an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers that is worse at night.

He has erythematous papules and pustules on the palms and soles, scattered papules over the trunk, and several nodules in the axillae and groin. There are burrows visible on the instep of the left foot. He has a low grade eczema history but this eruption looks different to his parents and has not responded to emollient and one percent hydrocortisone. He is feeding well and weight is tracking on the 25th centile. There is no fever and no honey coloured crusting.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on palms and soles, burrows on the left instep, nodules in axillae and groin, scattered truncal papules, scalp spared of nodules, no crusting or cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Weight on the 25th centile, no laboratory tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for the infant?

options.text: Topical benzyl benzoate 25 percent applied to the body below the neck on three consecutive nights
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative scabicide but causes marked stinging and irritant dermatitis and requires dilution in young children, so it is not the preferred first agent in infancy. Restricting application to below the neck also misses the scalp and face, which are involved at this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Escalation to a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for the whole eruption
options.rationale: Corticosteroid suppresses the itch and the inflammatory response while the mites continue to multiply, producing the modified and often widespread picture sometimes called incognito scabies. It has a place only after scabicidal treatment for the residual post scabetic itch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral cefalexin suspension for seven days to treat presumed bacterial infection of the pustular lesions
options.rationale: Pustules in infantile scabies are usually sterile and part of the infestation rather than bacterial superinfection, which would show honey coloured crusting, warmth or cellulitis. Antibiotics are added only when those secondary features are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Topical permethrin 5 percent applied to the whole body including scalp, with all contacts treated
options.rationale: Palmoplantar pustules, burrows and axillary nodules with an itchy household contact is scabies, and permethrin 5 percent is the preferred agent in Australia and may be used from the neonatal period under medical supervision. Infants differ from adults in that the scalp, face, neck, palms and soles must all be treated, and simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents immediate reinfestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral ivermectin given as a single weight based dose with a repeat dose after seven days elapse
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is not used in infants below 15 kg because safety at low body weight has not been established, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks and treatment failure. The weight here is far below that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult presentation in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically have palmar and plantar involvement with pustules, nodules in the axillae and groin, and involvement of the scalp, face and neck, all sites that are typically spared in adults. Diagnosis is clinical, strongly supported by an intensely itchy household contact with the classic nocturnal itch, and burrows are the pathognomonic lesion. Permethrin 5 percent is the Australian first line agent and can be used in young infants under medical supervision, applied to the entire body surface including the scalp and face in this age group, with all household and close contacts treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for two to four weeks after successful eradication, and this post scabetic itch should be treated symptomatically rather than being read as treatment failure.
key_points: Infantile scabies involves palms, soles, scalp and face, unlike the adult distribution
Permethrin 5 percent is first line and covers the whole body including the scalp in infants
All household and close contacts are treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms
Oral ivermectin is avoided below 15 kg and is reserved for crusted disease or failure
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and is not evidence of treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Reserve a second permethrin application for seven days after the first, since the agent is not fully ovicidal and a repeat treatment kills mites hatching from surviving eggs, while treating persistent itch at three weeks with repeated scabicide instead of an emollient and a short corticosteroid course causes irritant dermatitis that is then mistaken for continuing infestation.

subtopic_detail: Sharply marginated perioral and perineal erosions with diarrhoea in a breastfed preterm infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old girl born at 30 weeks gestation, now exclusively breastfed, referred with a nappy rash that has not responded to two weeks of topical antifungal treatment and barrier cream.

Her mother describes loose stools most days for a month and says her daughter has become irritable and has stopped rolling, which she had been doing at three months. There are sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with erosion and scale around the mouth, on the perineum extending onto the buttocks, and on the fingertips and around both heels. There are no satellite pustules. The scalp hair looks sparse and lighter than in her photographs from a month ago. Her mother is well, takes no supplements and eats a mixed diet. Two other infants in the practice with candidal nappy rash responded to the same antifungal cream within a week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142/min, BP 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sharply marginated erosive plaques periorally, perineally with buttock extension, on fingertips and around the heels, no satellite lesions, sparse lightened scalp hair, weight crossed from the 25th to below the 3rd centile since two months of age
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (100-135), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), immunoglobulin levels within normal limits, alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L (children 100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a nystatin and hydrocortisone combination preparation with strict barrier cream application
options.rationale: Candidal nappy rash involves the skin folds with satellite pustules and responds to antifungal treatment, neither of which fits a rash that has failed two weeks of therapy and extends to the mouth, fingertips and heels. Adding a corticosteroid treats inflammation without correcting the underlying deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash)

options.text: Refer for skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence to investigate an autoimmune blistering disorder
options.rationale: Immunobullous disease in infancy is rare and presents with tense blisters and erosions in a distribution not confined to periorificial and acral sites, without the systemic triad seen here. Biopsy delays a treatment that would produce a visible response within days. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

options.text: Commence an extensively hydrolysed formula trial for suspected cow milk protein allergy with review
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy in an exclusively breastfed infant is managed by maternal dietary exclusion rather than formula, and it does not produce sharply marginated acral erosions or hair depigmentation. The rash distribution is the finding that does not fit an allergic enteropathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.text: Arrange sweat chloride testing and faecal elastase measurement to investigate for cystic fibrosis
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis can present with a zinc responsive rash through malabsorption and deserves consideration, but newborn screening covers the great majority of Australian infants and the rash still requires zinc replacement whatever the cause. Testing without treating leaves a rapidly correctable deficiency unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

options.text: Measure serum zinc with albumin and start empirical elemental zinc supplementation while awaiting it
options.rationale: An acral and periorificial erosive eruption resistant to antifungals, with diarrhoea, sparse lightening hair, developmental regression and faltering growth, is the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and hair change that defines zinc deficiency, and the low alkaline phosphatase is a supportive clue because that enzyme is zinc dependent. Treatment is started before the level returns because the clinical response within days is itself confirmatory and the deficiency is rapidly reversible. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

explanation.summary: Zinc deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant arises either from an inherited defect of intestinal zinc absorption or, distinctively, from a maternal defect in the mammary zinc transporter that produces breast milk of abnormally low zinc content in an entirely well mother. Preterm infants are at particular risk because most zinc is accrued in the third trimester and their requirements per kilogram are high. The clinical signature is a sharply marginated erosive eruption in periorificial and acral distribution that fails antifungal and barrier treatment, together with diarrhoea, irritability, developmental regression, faltering growth and sparse depigmenting hair. A low serum alkaline phosphatase is a useful supporting clue because the enzyme requires zinc, and serum zinc should be interpreted alongside albumin since zinc is largely protein bound and hypoalbuminaemia lowers the measured value. Supplementation is started empirically because the dermatological response within days is both therapeutic and diagnostic.
key_points: Periorificial plus acral erosions failing antifungal therapy is the pattern to recognise
Preterm infants have low zinc stores because accrual is a third trimester event
A well mother can produce zinc deficient milk through a mammary transporter defect
Low alkaline phosphatase supports the diagnosis because the enzyme is zinc dependent
Interpret serum zinc alongside albumin and treat empirically rather than waiting
explanation.pearls: Measure zinc in the mother's breast milk rather than her serum when an exclusively breastfed infant responds to supplementation, because a maternal SLC30A2 mammary transporter defect leaves her own serum zinc and her health entirely normal, and identifying it changes counselling for any subsequent infant she breastfeeds.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy
